input: In this study, the adsorption of a dye from water onto a metal-organic framework was investigated in a series of batch tests, which were carried out at 298 K. The results were analysed using the Langmuir model, and the fitted Langmuir capacity was found to be 205 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5, which highlights the considerable capacity of the material under the conditions studied. In further experiments, an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1 was used, and it was observed that removal after 120 min reached 82% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, meaning that the concentration was brought down to a residual level of 9 mg L-1. It is important to note, however, that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only, and the capacity at other pH values was not measured, so care should be taken when generalising these findings beyond the conditions that were actually examined. The performance of the adsorbent may well vary across the wider range of conditions that could be encountered in practice, and the figures obtained here relate specifically to the tested condition at pH 5, where the solution chemistry, the dose, and the contact time all came together in the particular combination that was examined during the course of this work. The batch method that was used allowed each test to be run under closely controlled conditions, with the adsorbent brought into contact with the dye solution and the two then separated once the contact period had elapsed, after which the remaining dye in the solution was measured in order to establish how much had been taken up by the material during the test.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity at pH 5 was 205 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 82% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, leaving a residual concentration of 9 mg L-1. The capacity is a fitted parameter of the Langmuir model applied to the batch data, and it states the loading the model reaches as concentration rises; it is not a loading measured at a single concentration. The removal figure belongs to its own conditions as a bundle: dose, contact time, and initial concentration stand together, and a change in any of them takes the result outside the measured set. Both results were obtained at the tested pH, and the Langmuir fit is reported for that pH only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, so neither figure extends beyond pH 5. Dye uptake on an adsorbent of this kind is set in part by the charge state of the surface and of the dye, both of which move with pH, and an unmeasured pH is an unmeasured capacity. The passage therefore supports comparison with other materials tested at pH 5 under the same dose and contact time, and it supports no claim about performance in a stream whose pH differs from the tested value. The batch arrangement behind the figures matters to their use: the adsorbent and the solution are brought together for the stated contact period and then separated, and the measurement is of the solution that remains. A continuous stream, a mixed feed, or an adsorbent already carrying a loading from earlier use sits outside the arrangement tested, and the figures transfer to such a case only as an estimate whose error is unmeasured.
